item.title: 🔴 Patch Tuesday - October 2026
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Microsoft is publishing 1,413 own-product vulnerabilities on October 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Anyone who enjoyed last month’s record-setting Patch Tuesday will love the October 2026 edition, because it’s much bigger still. As Rapid7 has noted over the course of 2026, there is every reason to suppose that vulnerability volumes will continue to rise. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, as well as public disclosure for two others.

item.title: 🔴 Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-104935)
item.description:
Why this matters: Authentication bypass — review access controls and look for unauthorized access.

Overview

On October 13, 2026, Ivanti published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104935, a high-severity authentication bypass by spoofing (CWE-290) affecting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS). The vulnerability has a CVSSv3.0 score of 8.6 and allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands.

Ivanti reports that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers. This indicates that exploitation has been occurring as a zero-day vulnerability. item.title: 🔴 Critical infrastructure orgs face heightened cyber risk from nation-state groups, AI threats
item.description:
Why this matters: Advanced threat activity — review privileged access, persistence detection, and lateral-movement controls.

Critical infrastructure faces mounting threats from nation-state groups and AI-driven attacks. In the latest installment of our Cybersecurity Awareness Month blog series, learn how leading cybersecurity agencies, such as CISA, are advising critical infrastructure organizations on ways to protect themselves and the essential services they provide.

Key takeaways

  1. Critical infrastructure organizations often struggle with asset visibility gaps that create hidden attack vectors. Many older OT systems are difficult to inventory, leaving them unmonitored and unpatched.
  2. Attackers are leveraging AI to map converged IT/OT networks at machine speed and exploit uninventoried legacy systems. Attackers are also using AI to attain the specialized know-how to breach complex industrial control systems.
  3. Iran-affiliated APT groups have attacked U.S. water, energy, and government facilities since the U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury in February, according to the U.S. government.
  4. As part of Cybersecurity Awareness Month, CISA is urging critical infrastructure operators to establish a solid cyber hygiene foundation, anchored on reducing vulnerabilities, replacing unsupported legacy devices, and preparing rapid recovery plans.

item.title: 🔴 CVE-2026-97229: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in GitLab
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Overview

On October 12, 2026, GitLab published a critical patch release for CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow or wraparound (CWE-190) in the CI/CD regular expression compiler affecting GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). GitLab assigned the vulnerability a CVSSv3.1 score of 10.0. Under certain conditions, a remote attacker can execute arbitrary code on an affected GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression stored in a malicious CI/CD configuration. While the vendor supplied CVSS score indicates that exploitation is fully unauthenticated, in reproducing the exploit it was noted that an attacker must have a mechanism to plant a malicious CI/CD configuration to a repository prior to triggering…

Tenable uses Tenable One AI Exposure to screen for prompt injection and exposed secrets, and OpenAI GPT Cyber models to assess the code and threat model. item.title: 🔴 Four compliance frameworks, one security team: Why fragmented university security raises regulatory risk
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

In Part 1 of this series, we looked at the security challenges created by fragmented, campus-by-campus environments. Higher education also faces a second pressure that makes that fragmentation harder to sustain: overlapping compliance obligations across FERPA, GLBA, HIPAA, and CMMC.

Each framework brings different requirements, reporting timelines, and consequences for failure. Managing them across one institution is already complex, but across a multi-campus university system with separate tools, staff, data stores, and governance practices, it becomes much harder to establish what happened, what data was involved, and which reporting requirements apply. With universities already facing an average of 4,388 cyberattacks per organization per week, according to the figures cited in Part 1, that regulatory complexity is becoming an operational security problem as much as a compliance one.

FERPA puts universities on a 24-hour clock

The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act has governed the privacy of student education records since 1974, but the pressure on security teams becomes much more immediate when financial aid information is involved. item.title: 🟠 The ASOS Incident: When Attackers Use the Channels Customers Trust
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

This week, ASOS customers opened their phones to find a hostile push notification delivered through the retailer’s own app. The message claimed the company’s Snowflake environment had been compromised and directed ASOS to engage with the sender through Telegram. ASOS later confirmed to Sky News that an unauthorized customer notification had been sent and said it was investigating activity involving third-party platforms used to communicate with customers. The company also said basic personal information, including names and contact details, may have been accessed, while payment-card information and account passwords were not believed to be affected.

The attackers’ wider claims remain unverified, and Snowflake told Sky News that its investigation had found no compromise of the Snowflake platform at that point. Even without knowing the full route into ASOS’s environment, though, the notification raises a useful question for security teams: what happens when an attacker can communicate through a channel customers already trust?
